title: Presence, Social Capital, Social Isolation in Virtual Environments: The Role of Extraversion in Shaping Relational Outcomes
authors: Dohyeon Kim, Kyungmin Kim, Hun Kim
abstract: Virtual environment communication has been increasingly discussed as a potential means of addressing social isolation, yet little is known about how different forms of presence become relational resources. This study examines how physical presence and social presence in virtual environments are associated with social isolation through virtual-environment bonding and bridging social capital, and whether these relationships differ by users’ level of extraversion. Data were collected from 500 Korean adults with experience using ZEPETO and analyzed using CB-SEM and multi-group analysis. The results show that physical presence is positively associated with both bonding and bridging social capital, suggesting that perceived realism is associated with both forms of relational resources. Social presence is negatively associated with bonding social capital but positively associated with bridging social capital, indicating that the sense of being with others may be more closely associated with weak-tie expansion rather than close relational cohesion. Bonding social capital is positively associated with social isolation, whereas bridging social capital is not significantly associated with social isolation in the overall model. Multi-group analysis revealed that the positive association between bonding social capital and social isolation was significantly stronger among extraverted users. Bridging social capital was negatively associated with social isolation only in the extraversion group, although the between-group difference was not statistically significant at the 0.05 level. These findings suggest that the socio-psychological outcomes associated with VE-Comm vary not simply on the overall level of presence, but on the type of presence, the form of social capital reported, and users’ personality traits.

title: Affordances-based resistance to digital surveillance
authors: Alessandro Caliandro, Ilir Rama, Veronica Moretti
abstract: This article introduces the notion of affordances-based resistance to digital surveillance as a practice mediated by the socio-technical architecture of digital platforms: a type of countersurveillance that is not organised or structured by the norms and practices of social and political movements, but is instead structured and held together by the technical features of digital media and the participatory cultures thriving on them. Specifically, we consider this resistance passive and mechanical because it is: driven by the affordances (and not resulting from an active manipulation of them); individualised and dispersed on a large scale, not localised in or governed by traditional social organisations (e.g. civic associations); and a form of resistance in which actors are more nudged towards resistance behaviours than deliberately pursuing them. To illustrate, we develop a cross-platform analysis of Twitter and the Google Play Store, examining 270,656 tweets and 23,469 reviews about the contact tracing app Immuni. The article contributes by introducing a novel concept for studying resistance to datafication and by proposing a methodological approach linking low- and high-level affordances through cross-platform analysis.

title: AI Chatbot’s Self-Confidence Cues Shape Users’ Impressions of the Chatbot, but Not Accuracy Judgments of Hallucinated Responses

title: Love Takes Time: Faster Romantic Onset, Lower Closeness, and Similarity Benefits in Human-AI Relationships
authors: Jiahui Liu, Rabindra Ratan, David Markowitz, Dayeoun Jang
journal_full: Journal of Language and Social Psychology
abstract: As human–artificial intelligence (AI) romantic relationships become increasingly prevalent, understanding how they develop is important. Such relationships differ from human–human relationships in how AI partners accommodate user needs and preferences, potentially influencing relationship development and closeness. In this survey ( N = 167), individuals who reported falling in love more quickly with human partners also tended to do so with AI partners. However, paired within-subject analyses ( n = 110) revealed that participants perceived a faster overall pace of falling in love with AI than human partners, driven primarily by shorter conversation lengths rather than fewer days or total conversations. Despite this expediency, participants reported greater current relational closeness with human partners than AI partners. Perceived similarity with AI partners was positively associated with relational closeness and relationship quality with AI. These findings suggest that human–AI romantic relationships may develop rapidly through familiar interpersonal processes such as similarity attraction, yet involve lower relational closeness.

title: From Communication Anxiety to Psychological Reliance
authors: Mina Choi, Hyesun Choung, Inyoung Shin, Samuel Hardman Taylor
abstract: Abstract: Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), this study investigates how communication anxiety and psychological need satisfaction relate to the use of Large Language Model (LLM)-based chatbots, specifically ChatGPT, for communication tasks (e.g., writing emails, drafting messages, and preparing scripts). Using a three-wave panel survey of participants from the United States and South Korea, we examined both between- and within-person dynamics. Results showed that individuals with higher trait-level communication anxiety tended to use ChatGPT more frequently for communication tasks, whereas within-person fluctuations in anxiety did not predict greater use. ChatGPT use was positively associated with the satisfaction of basic psychological needs – autonomy, competence, and relatedness – and this need satisfaction, in turn, was associated with greater psychological reliance on ChatGPT. Importantly, need satisfaction further mediated the relationship between ChatGPT use and psychological reliance at both within- and between-person levels. Cultural comparisons revealed that US participants exhibited stronger momentary effects, while Korean participants showed more stable, trait-based patterns. These findings highlight the role of LLM-based chatbots as need-supportive communication tools that may become integrated into users’ communication practices over time, with implications for theories of AI-mediated communication, cross-cultural research, and the design of human-AI communication systems.

title: Testing the Parasocial Contact Hypothesis Through Stand-Up Comedy
authors: John A. Banas, Elena Bessarabova, Doris Acheme, Valerie Biwa, Norman Wong
abstract: Abstract: The study examined how humorous parasocial contact can reduce prejudice toward outgroups. Study predictions were tested in an experiment ( N = 301) comparing the effects of a comedy stand-up by a Muslim comedian (Hasan Minhaj or Mohammed Amer) to a control condition a stand-up from a non-Muslim comedian (Brian Regan or Jim Gaffigan). Results indicated that humorous parasocial contact was effective at facilitating parasocial relationships in all conditions. Consistent with study predictions, when participants were exposed to the mediated intergroup contact with a Muslim comedian, parasocial relationships – mediated through intergroup anxiety – were positively associated with willingness for contacts with Muslims (i.e., negatively associated with social distance) and negatively associated with endorsement of Muslim stereotypes. In contrast, these mediational relationships were not observed when mediated intergroup contact occurred with a White comedian. These and other results are discussed along with implications, limitations, and future research directions.

title: Prioritizing Journalistic Norms or Humanitarian Values? A Multistage Computational Analysis of Journalistic Role Performance in Humanitarian News
authors: Zhe Xu, Martin Scott, Dani Madrid-Morales, Kate Wright, Shuai Wang
abstract: This study examines how journalistic roles are performed in humanitarian news. Using a multistage computational approach applied to news data from 46 international news organizations across 21 countries, we find that role performance varies systematically across topics, political systems, and organizational types. Our findings complicate the predominant tendency in humanitarian journalism scholarship to frame roles in terms of professional norms or humanitarian values. Instead, we show that role performance is multidimensional and contextually contingent. Improving humanitarian coverage therefore requires attention not only to professional practices but also to the institutional conditions that enable diverse forms of journalism.

title: When Epistemic Authority Collapses: Linking Fake News Media Perception and Conspiracy Beliefs to Disinformation Vulnerability
authors: Alberto Ardèvol-Abreu, Alberto E. López-Carrión, Jenny del Pino García Sánchez
abstract: Citizens increasingly need to detect and filter disinformation, yet we know little about why some are more vulnerable than others. We examine whether forms of skepticism toward traditional epistemic authorities—fake news media perception (FNMP) and conspiracy beliefs—are associated with disinformation vulnerability. Using two-wave survey data from Spain ( N W1 = 1,207; n W2 = 821), we find that FNMP is widespread, not a fringe phenomenon. Conspiracy beliefs predict vulnerability across cross-sectional, lagged, and autoregressive models. Support for FNMP as a predictor is partial and not sustained in autoregressive models. Evidence for the interaction between FNMP and conspiracy beliefs is weak.

title: TikTok News: How The Washington Post ’s Use of Platform Logics Affects Perceptions of Journalists and News Learning
authors: Audrey Halversen, Brian E. Weeks
abstract: In a period of high competition, many contemporary journalists attract audience attention by adopting the stylistic conventions (“logics”) of platforms like TikTok to deliver news online. However, the effects of this content on audience trust and learning remain unclear. Using two online experiments, we examine whether audiences perceive journalists as credible and learn from news videos employing TikTok logics, compared to traditional print articles. Results indicate that journalists using TikTok logics may effectively capture attention but are viewed as less trustworthy, credible, professional, and knowledgeable, though more likable, than print journalists. Learning outcomes are similar across formats.

title: Which Is the Antecedent: Loneliness or Problematic Mobile Phone Use? Evidence from the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model and Cross-Lagged Panel Network Analysis
authors: Mengmeng Zhang, Xiantong Yang
abstract: Despite growing evidence linking loneliness with problematic mobile phone use (PMPU), the temporal direction between these constructs remains debated. Drawing on the cognitive-behavioral model of pathological Internet use and the compensatory Internet use theory, loneliness is theorized to increase PMPU as a coping strategy for social isolation, whereas the displacement hypothesis suggests that PMPU may instead serve as an antecedent of loneliness. To resolve this theoretical inconsistency, we examined both variable- and symptom-level associations between loneliness and PMPU using the random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) and cross-lagged panel network analysis (CLPN). A total of 768 adolescents completed three assessments at approximately 6-month intervals over 1 year. The RI-CLPM revealed bidirectional within-person associations: higher loneliness predicted greater subsequent PMPU, and elevated PMPU predicted increased loneliness over time. The CLPN further uncovered the strongest cross-lagged edges were all from loneliness to PMPU symptoms. Additionally, several key nodes in the network were identified. From T1 to T2, PMPU5 ( friends/family complaint ) showed the highest out-EI and PMPU9 ( excessive duration notification ) had the highest in-EI; from T2 to T3, PMPU6 ( unexpected usage duration ) showed the highest out-EI and PMPU4 ( mobile check anxiety ) had the highest in-EI. These findings highlight the importance of integrating variable- and symptom-level approaches to advance theoretical understanding of the dynamic association between loneliness and PMPU and to inform practical interventions that help break this vicious cycle among adolescents.

title: “I Share Your Sentiment”—A Longitudinal Study of Facebook Post Sentiment and Sharing
authors: Anders Olof Larsson
abstract: This study examines how Norwegian political parties used negative, positive or neutral sentiment on Facebook over a 10-year period (2016–2025) and how such sentiment affected the sharing of their posts. Drawing on a full population of posts from all major parliamentary parties, the study investigates (a) whether negative sentiment increases over time, (b) how sentiment varies with party ideology and incumbency status, and (c) how positive and negative sentiment relate to sharing overall and at the party level. Demonstrating an approach using large language models in combination with human annotation for sentiment analysis, the study finds that while positive sentiment remains dominant, negative sentiment has increased over time, especially among challenger and left-wing parties. Extremist parties on both the far-left and far-right post more negative content, but this does not consistently translate into higher sharing. Overall, negative posts tend to receive more shares, but this advantage appears to weaken over time, suggesting strategic adaptation and possible audience fatigue.

title: Scripts of Escalation and Restraint: State Messaging and Public Opinion in International Crises
authors: Frances Yaping Wang
abstract: Public opinion can both enable and constrain foreign policy, motivating governments to manipulate media during international crises. This study identifies four recurring communication strategies, one mobilizing and three moderating, each organized around a dominant cue: mobilization relies primarily on emotional arousal to stoke nationalist sentiment and foster assertiveness; censorship centers on the informational restriction of politically sensitive content; delegitimization uses normative appeals to discredit hawkish responses as irresponsible or illegitimate; and posturing employs performative displays of toughness intended to make moderate policies politically acceptable. Using a large-scale survey experiment in China, Vietnam, and the Philippines, the study evaluates how these strategies affect the public’s foreign-policy preferences and tolerance for policy deviation in a simulated fishing dispute in the South China Sea. The results show that mobilization shifts preferences in a more hawkish direction and reduces tolerance for deviation, whereas delegitimization consistently steers the public toward more moderate foreign policy preferences across countries. Censorship tempers policy preferences in all three countries but is strongest in Vietnam; posturing has no significant effect in China or Vietnam and produces a more hawkish response in the Philippines. Although the sources of this cross-national heterogeneity cannot be definitively identified, the findings suggest that propaganda effectiveness may depend partly on how audiences interpret different messages. Explicitly prescriptive strategies, such as mobilization and delegitimization, appear more portable across contexts, whereas informational or performative strategies, such as censorship and posturing, may be more contingent on audience predispositions, including baseline hawkishness, and on broader political and informational environments.

title: Campaigning on emotion: Party strategy and emotional appeals in the 2024 UK general election
authors: Iván Sánchez-Marañón, Jordi Rodríguez-Virgili, Miguel Gómez-Irimia
abstract: Purpose: This article examines how political parties used emotional appeals in campaign advertising during the 2024 United Kingdom general election. Methods: Through content analysis of ads published by the Conservative Party, Labour, the Liberal Democrats, and Reform UK across their main social media platforms, we identify party-level patterns in emotional strategy and the conditions shaping their use. Findings: The Conservative Party relied heavily on fear, consistent with its trailing incumbent status. Labour led on anger, directing appeals almost exclusively at the Conservative governing record, while also deploying enthusiasm around the promise of change. Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats made the most frequent use of enthusiasm. Across all parties, enthusiasm targeted the ingroup, while anger and fear targeted the outgroup. Conclusions: These findings align with theoretical expectations derived from incumbency status and poll position across a full field of competing parties in a single campaign, providing evidence that electoral periods fuel affective polarisation.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Surveys
authors: Yamil Velez, Alec Ewig
abstract: We introduce retrieval-augmented surveys, a novel survey approach that links respondents’ open-ended priorities to concrete policy proposals in institutional databases, enabling personalized measures of how citizens’ concerns map onto formal agendas. Our pipeline elicits and clarifies each respondent’s top issue concern, summarizes items in a policy database and retrieves semantically relevant candidates (“nearest neighbors”) for inclusion in a respondent-tailored survey. We illustrate the approach with an application to political representation in Congress, evaluating performance across four metrics. First, large majorities of respondents judge the retrieved policy items as mostly or fully addressing their concerns. Second, a hand-coding audit corroborates the alignment of retrieved items with respondent issue stances. Third, support for retrieved items is stable over a short-term panel, with 82% of respondents at the top of the support scale remaining there three weeks later. Fourth, in a tailored conjoint, alignment on the nearest neighbor item has a larger estimated effect on candidate choice than benchmark policies. The framework is modular and portable to other settings, such as rulemaking, municipal agendas, and public budgets, enabling scholars to identify where representation succeeds or fails in the institutional pipeline.

title: An Image Is Worth K Topics: A Visual Structural Topic Model with Pretrained Image Embeddings
authors: Matías Piqueras, Alexandra Segerberg, Matteo Magnani, Måns Magnusson, Nataša Sladoje
abstract: Political scientists are increasingly interested in analyzing visual content at scale. However, the existing computational toolbox is still in need of methods and models attuned to the specific challenges and goals of social and political inquiry. In this article, we introduce a visual structural topic model (vSTM) that combines continuous image embeddings with a structural topic model. This has important advantages compared to existing approaches. First, continuous embeddings allow the model to capture the semantic complexity of images, which is relevant to the study of politics. A consequence of using continuous embeddings is that we can directly use off-the-shelf pretrained deep learning models, offering state-of-the-art performance in image analysis tasks while saving time, cost and resources. Second, the structural topic model provides the ability to analyze how topics and covariates are related, while maintaining a nuanced representation of images as a mixture of multiple topics. In our experiments, we show that the vSTM is able to identify topics that are interpretable, coherent and relevant to the study of online political communication.

title: The rhythm of persuasion: Media channels, psychological priming, and voting decisions through political music in Nigeria
authors: Ukamaka C. M. Ozioko, Success Esomchi Obi, Anibueze U. Anselm, Agaba Joseph David, Chinasa Emelda Nnanyelugo, Charles Chukwudi Eze, Jude Chukwudi Agbo, Gever Verlumun Celestine
abstract: The objective of this study was to determine the effect of exposure to political music on voting decisions among Nigerian voters. Data were collected from a multistage sample of 388 participants, and logistic and linear regression models were applied to evaluate the hypotheses. The findings revealed that an individual's overall exposure to political music significantly predicts their likelihood of voting, demonstrating a small positive effect size (Odds Ratio = 1.08). Rather than operating through indirect moderation pathways, exposure media and geographic location emerged as the strongest direct predictors of persuasive influence. Specifically, direct exposure via local radio ( β = .21) and shared audio files ( β = .12) significantly predicted a voter's influence score. Furthermore, rural voters reported being significantly more influenced by political music than their urban counterparts, with geographic location operating as the strongest overall direct baseline predictor ( β = −.48). The study concludes that the psychological effectiveness of political music lies not in generalized, blanket exposure, but in a targeted strategic focus that leverages specific media channels and subcultural demographic segments to maximize persuasive impact on voter behavior.

title: Cult of Personality or Lack of Competition? Determining Trump’s Sway Over Republican Partisans on a Critical Case
authors: Love Christensen, Mattias Agerberg
abstract: It is well established that partisans follow their leaders. While this potentially has important implications for political accountability, studies of opinion leadership rarely examine accountability directly. We test whether partisans are able to hold a dominant leader accountable under favorable conditions using a critical case: Trump’s position on the Epstein files. Two preregistered experiments, fielded before the release of the Epstein files, show that partisans follow Trump and do not hold him accountable when he is unopposed or contested by the Democrats. However, when Trump faces opposition from within his own bloc—especially countermessaging from right-coded media elites—both issue-specific and overall approval decline substantially, and following is halved. Our results have two important implications. First, opinion leadership does not imply the absence of political accountability. Second, meaningful political competition in polarized societies may need to originate from within ideological blocs. While Trump is powerful, credible opposition can make him accountable.

title: Agreement Helps, Disagreement Matters: Scaling Framing Function Annotation With Large Language Models
authors: Emily Robinson, Ranadheer Malla, Chico Q. Camargo
abstract: Framing research has long relied on human annotation, but many aspects of framing – especially framing functions such as defining problems, identifying causes, making moral evaluations, or proposing solutions are difficult to label consistently and at scale. We demonstrate that large language models can reliably identify these framing functions, achieving levels of agreement comparable to those of human annotators. We evaluate three state-of-the-art models (GPT-5, Claude 3.7, and DeepSeek) alongside three trained human coders on a new dataset of social media posts about electric-vehicles, a highly topical and contested issue that holds many interpretations. This setting provides a strong test of both agreement and meaningful disagreement in framing-function annotation. Across models and humans, we find not only substantial convergence but also patterns of valid disagreement – differences that reflect legitimate alternative interpretations rather than annotation error. Recognising and preserving these cases enhances construct validity and provides a more realistic portrayal of how framing functions operate in contested debates. Our results demonstrate that large language models can scale framing function analysis while capturing the variability inherent in human interpretation, enabling forms of communication research that were previously impractical with human-only coding.

title: Who Goes Toxic? Understanding Political Toxicity on Social Media Across Individuals and Contexts
authors: Alon Zoizner, Nir Lotan, Sagi Pendzel, Einat Minkov
abstract: As political toxicity has become widespread on social media, scholars have sought to understand what drives it. While studies often emphasize platform-level explanations, such as algorithmic amplification, they offer limited insight into which users are more likely to produce toxic content. Even less is known about how the relationship between individual-level factors and toxicity varies across political contexts. Using data from 184,354 randomly sampled U.S. Twitter (now X) users, their original tweets (25M), and the accounts they follow, we link users’ inferred characteristics and political context to their real-life toxic behavior. Results show that Republican, male, and older users are consistently more likely to post both impolite and intolerant content, whereas education shows no clear association. We also find that state-level electoral competitiveness increases overall toxicity and, in some cases, conditions individual-level relationships. The age gap in impolite behavior significantly narrows in more competitive states, while the corresponding moderation for intolerance is only marginally significant. There is also some indication that partisan differences in impoliteness become larger in more competitive states, but this moderation is only marginally significant. Together, these results demonstrate that political toxicity is shaped jointly by users’ individual characteristics and the political contexts in which they operate.
